blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Preference tuning of text-to-image diffusion models spends most of its compute generating candidate images, yet training prompts are typically sampled uniformly at random, wasting compute generating images that provide too little signal for model alignment. To best utilize the available compute, we study prompt selection, where at each iteration we identify the most useful prompts for preference tuning. We separate prompt selection into a utility score, an estimator of that utility score, and batch selection. Within this framework, we propose Selection by PRedicting Objective-grounded UTility (SPROUT). The utility score is predicted on every prompt in the pool, including unseen prompts, by a text-only model, refit after every iteration on all utilities observed so far. A randomized acceptance rule then turns these predictions into a batch, so no images are generated beyond those used for training. For direct group preference optimization (DGPO), the objective-grounded utility is the norm of the gradient that the objective produces from a prompt's group of images. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 with DGPO on GenEval, SPROUT matches the final score of uniform sampling in about 44% of the iterations and improves the area under the learning curve with respect to both uniform sampling and CGPO, a recent variance-based prompt sampler. The efficiency gains hold under four held-out reward models never used in training, and the ranking of methods carries over to DPG-Bench and T2I-CompBench++. Our code is available at https://github.com/ADDAPT-ML/SPROUT.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Preference tuning has become a standard approach to align generative models with human
judgment, including text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models, where we collect comparisons between generated images and tune the model toward the preferred
ones ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ) . The comparisons can come from human annotators, from learned reward models, or from hand-crafted reward pipelines such as GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , which makes the procedure cheap enough to iterate.

blocks.en:
While assigning reward scores has become more efficient, generating images to be scored remains expensive. Aligning a diffusion model requires generating
multiple images per prompt, scoring them, and computing a gradient update on the scored generated images, so the cost of an iteration is linear in the number of prompts: doubling the prompts per iteration doubles the time and computation of preference tuning. Generating and scoring the images also takes more than half of an iteration in our runs (about 56%, Appendix A ), so the cost of a prompt is avoided only if the prompt is discarded before generation.

在分配奖励分数的效率提高的同时,生成要打分的图像仍然昂贵. 调整扩散模型需要生成
每个快取多的图像,打分,并在得分生成的图像上计算出一个梯度更新,因此一个迭代的成本在快取数上是线性:每迭代的快取数增加一倍,优先调值的计算时间和偏好调值. 生成和评分图像也占用了我们运行中一半以上的迭代(约56%,附录A),因此只有在生成前即被丢弃时,才避免了即时的成本.

blocks.en:
This generation cost motivates prompt selection: not all prompts are equally worth generating from.
A prompt
whose candidates come out uniformly strong, or uniformly weak, yields a poorly separated comparison and
contributes little, yet consumes the same generation budget as one that yields a well-separated group.
Identifying the useful prompts before generating can reduce the computational cost directly. We call this the prompt selection problem.

blocks.en:
Active learning is one precedent ( MacKay, 1992 ; Lewis and Gale, 1994 ; Sener and Savarese, 2018 ; Kirsch et al., 2019 ) ,
but the resource it conserves is annotation of data that already exists. Here the data do not exist
until they are paid for, and the resource is generation , so a prompt selection algorithm has to predict
the value of a sample it has not yet seen. Closer to our setting, prompt curricula in reinforcement learning select or filter prompts before or during generation ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Foster et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Bu et al., 2026 ) .
The closest to our setting, CGPO ( Li et al., 2026a ) , samples text-to-image prompts by a prompt-specific estimate of the reward variance, which cannot distinguish among prompts that have not been generated from, the vast majority of a large prompt pool. More generally, a reward statistic is not directly tied to how the preference objective uses a prompt’s images ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Qu et al., 2026b ; Qu et al., 2026a ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ) , and probe generations spend the budget that selection is meant to save ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en: In this work, we propose SPROUT ( S election by PR edicting O bjective-grounded UT ility), which selects prompts by what the preference objective does with them rather than by a statistic of the reward. After each training iteration, every selected prompt receives a label: the norm of the gradient that the objective produces from its group of images, a by-product of the training step that costs no extra generation. A text-only utility model , refit online on all labels observed so far, generalizes these labels to every prompt in the pool, including prompts never generated from. Its predictions are then scaled to be acceptance probabilities, so that the next batch favors high-utility prompts while no prompts are completely excluded (Figure 1 ).

blocks.en: Our contributions are: • A text-only utility model, refit online, that estimates the utility of every prompt in the pool from its text. • An objective-grounded utility: the norm of the per-prompt gradient produced by the preference objective. • An evaluation on Stable Diffusion 1.5 tuned with DGPO on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , where our method reduces the training iterations needed to reach uniform sampling’s final score by a factor of 2.27 2.27 (the reduction factor , which measures the training that a given score requires), improves the area under the learning curve over uniform sampling and over CGPO ( Li et al., 2026a ) at no extra generation cost, and keeps its advantage under four held-out reward models ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Schuhmann et al., 2022 ; Schuhmann, 2022 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) and on DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) and T2I-CompBench++ ( Huang et al., 2025 ) .

blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Preference optimization tuning. DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) removes the explicit reward model of preference tuning with PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ziegler et al., 2019 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and Diffusion-DPO ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) adapts it to diffusion. Reward-backpropagation methods differentiate through sampling ( Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) , DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) applies reinforcement learning to diffusion, and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , Dr.GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) and DGPO ( Luo et al., 2026 ) compare rewards within a per-prompt group, across reasoning and visual generation.
However, they all assume a prompt distribution is given or use uniform prompt selection, and none of them asks which prompts to spend generation time and compute on.

blocks.en: Text-to-image prompt selection. FiFA ( Yang et al., 2025 ) filters an offline human-feedback dataset by preference margin, text quality, and diversity, and UniFL ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) selects informative and diverse prompts once before training, with a semantic filter and nearest-neighbor compression rather than a learned score. These methods are offline and the prompt selection does not evolve with the growing model capabilities. AdaGRPO ( Bu et al., 2026 ) generates one probe image per candidate prompt and selects the candidate whose probe reward is closest to a capability anchor, a moving average of the rewards the model has recently obtained. However, this requires additional generations for selection that are not used for training. The work most similar to ours is CGPO ( Li et al., 2026a ) , which updates historical variance-based sampling probabilities from the training generations only but loses the opportunity to intelligently select among prompts that have not been generated from. SPROUT is online, requires no additional generations, and can also extrapolate to ungenerated prompts.
blocks.zh: 文本到图像的快速选择 。 FiFA(Yang等,2025年)通过偏好比值,文本质量和多样性过滤出一款离线的人类食回数据集,而UniFL(Zhang等,2024年)在训练前选择一次信息化和多样的提示,使用语义过滤并进行近邻压缩而不是学习分数. 这些方法已下线,快速选择不会随着模型能力的不断增长而演变. AdaGRPO(Bu等,2026年)每个候选人生成一幅探测图像,并迅速选择其探测奖励最接近能力锚点的候选人,这是该模型最近获得的奖励的移动平均值. 然而,这需要更多的一代人来选择,而不是用来进行培训。 与我们最相近的作品是CGPO(Li等,2026a.),它仅更新了训练世代的历史差异性采样概率,却失去了在尚未从中产生的提示中明智选择的机会. SPROUT是在线的,不需要额外的代号,也可以推断为未生成的提示.

blocks.en: Learned utility models. MoPPS ( Qu et al., 2026a ) performs streaming Bayesian inference on each prompt’s success rate to avoid the rollout cost, a per-prompt estimate that does not generalize across prompts. GPS ( Qu et al., 2026b ) trains a small generative predictor on the shared optimization history and combines predicted difficulty with batch diversity, and PCL ( Gao et al., 2026 ) learns a value model of prompt success to hold a curriculum near intermediate difficulty. However, they are all in the LLM reasoning domain and use difficulty as the utility only. SPROUT instead uses the update the preference objective makes from a prompt as our learned utility, and to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to use a learned utility model for prompt selection in text-to-image preference tuning.
blocks.zh: 学习的公用事业模式。 MoPPS(Qu等, 2026a)对每个提示的成功率进行流派贝叶斯推论, GPS (Qu等, 2026b )在共享优化史上训练出一个小的基因预测器,并将预测难度与批量多样性相结合,PCL (Gao等, 2026) 学习了迅速成功的价值模型,将课程设置在接近中间难度的地方. 然而,它们都属于LLM推理领域,并且只使用难度作为效用. SPROUT则使用从我们学到的实用工具的即时更新的偏好目标,从我们学到的知识来看,我们第一个使用已学到的实用模式,在文本到图像偏好调制中迅速选择。

blocks.en:
Data selection. Active learning aims to determine what to label, where selecting
a batch to annotate can be as tricky as our batch prompt selection. Batch-aware Bayesian methods
address the redundancy that arises when top-scoring items are selected together ( Kirsch et al., 2019 ; Hu and Mussmann, 2025 ) , while stochastic batch
selection recovers much of that benefit by perturbing scores before top scoring ( Kirsch et al., 2023 ) .
Besides, Coreset selection ( Sener and Savarese, 2018 ) , prototypical multi-batch k k -means ( Pourahmadi et al., 2021 ) ,

These methods require access to the unlabeled data, whereas our setting requires selection before generating the unlabeled data.

blocks.en: We abstract online prompt selection into three separate components: a utility , the prompt-level quantity that selection should favor; an estimator , which scores candidate prompts by that utility; and batch selection , which uses the scores to select the B B prompts of an iteration. Existing methods correspond to particular choices of the three, which we review below; SPROUT (Section 4 ) contributes a new utility and a new estimator.

blocks.en: The difficulty and variance of Section 3.3 are both functions of the reward, and so are agnostic to the optimizer that actually updates the model. Once a group has been scored and trained on, the objective offers its own per-prompt quantity at no extra cost: the size of the gradient that the group produces. We define the update norm u t , i = log ⁡ ∥ g t , i ∥ median k ≤ B ⁡ ∥ g t , k ∥ , u_{t,i}=\log\frac{\lVert g_{t,i}\rVert}{\operatorname{median}_{k\leq B}\lVert g_{t,k}\rVert}, (4) where g t , i g_{t,i} is the gradient of the training loss with respect to the trainable parameters accumulated from prompt p t , i p_{t,i} ’s group at iteration t t , before gradient clipping. Normalizing by the batch median keeps labels from different iterations on a common scale, and the logarithm treats half and twice the median norm symmetrically, so that a few large gradients do not dominate the regression fit. blocks.en: 5.1 Data and reward models
blocks.zh: 5.1 数据和奖励模式

blocks.en:
To compare the empirical performance of prompt selection methods, we perform preference optimization with the GenEval prompts and reward, and evaluate the trained models via GenEval, held-out reward models, and other benchmarks.
Training prompts come from the GenEval training set released with DGPO ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , following the official implementation of Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025a ) ( 50,000 50{,}000 prompts), and the training reward is a partial-credit GenEval reward computed from the official detector’s per-requirement verdicts, inspired by Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , DGPO ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , and CGPO ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Evaluation follows the official GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) protocol: 553 553 prompts with four images each, macro-averaging the fraction of correct images over the six task categories. We also re-score the same evaluation images with four held-out reward models that never enter training: PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , HPS v2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , the LAION aesthetic predictor ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ; Schuhmann, 2022 ) and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) . Following CGPO, we also evaluate the GenEval-trained checkpoints on DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , and on T2I-CompBench++ ( Huang et al., 2025 ) .

blocks.en: Text-to-image models. We focus on low-budget, low-computation scenarios, which are often overlooked in preference tuning. We use Stable Diffusion 1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , a latent diffusion model, tuned with a LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) adapter. We follow DGPO’s released GenEval configuration, adapted to the Stable Diffusion 1.5 backbone, with a constant learning rate of 1.65 × 10 − 4 1.65\times 10^{-4} selected by a hyperparameter search with uniform sampling in preliminary experiments without using the test set. We train for T = 100 T=100 iterations, each with B = 8 B=8 prompts and G = 24 G=24 images per prompt, for a total of 19,200 generated training images. More details are in Appendix A .

Every method is trained with the same three seeds, fixed before any of the reported experiments, and we report means over the three seeds with “ ± \pm ” the half-width of the 95% confidence interval from the Student’s t t distribution. Differences between methods are paired on seed and reported as the mean with its 95% t t interval in brackets; bold marks intervals that exclude zero. The normalized area under the learning curve (nAULC) is the area under a benchmark’s learning curve, evaluated every 20 20 iterations from the base model (iteration 0 0 ) to iteration 100 100 , divided by 100 100 . The reduction factor is the iteration at which a baseline’s mean curve peaks divided by the iteration at which a method’s linearly interpolated mean curve first reaches that score, i.e., the factor by which the method reduces the training iterations needed for the baseline’s best score. Applied to each seed separately, SPROUT reaches uniform sampling’s best score on every seed, under every benchmark and held-out reward model (Appendix Table 4 ).

blocks.en: Main results. Figure 1 summarizes the reduction factors across benchmarks, Figure 3 (left, see Table 3 in the appendix for exact numbers) compares the methods on GenEval, and Table 7 in the appendix breaks the comparison down by task category, with example generations in Figure 4 . SPROUT reaches uniform sampling’s final GenEval score in less than half the iterations (a reduction factor of 2.27 × 2.27\times ) and its nAULC gain is significant against both uniform sampling ( + 0.0143 +0.0143 ) and CGPO ( + 0.0124 +0.0124 ). CGPO, in contrast, improves on uniform sampling only slightly, with an interval that includes zero: its per-prompt estimates are informed only by the prompts it has generated from, a small fraction of the pool when B × T ≪ | 𝒟 | B\times T\ll|\mathcal{D}| , whereas our utility model predicts the utility of every prompt at no extra generation cost. Figure 7 in Appendix E shows examples of prompts that the utility model ranks highest and lowest: images of a highest-ranked prompt receive more varied rewards than images of a lowest-ranked one, providing more useful training signal to preference optimization.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion and limitations
blocks.zh: 6. 结论和限制

blocks.en: We frame prompt selection for preference tuning of text-to-image models as three separate components — utility, estimator, and batch selection — and propose SPROUT, whose objective-grounded utility is the norm of the gradient that the preference objective produces from a prompt’s group. The utility is predicted from prompt text by a text-only model refit online, and prompts are accepted with probabilities scaled from the predicted utility. SPROUT reaches uniform sampling’s final GenEval score in less than half the iterations, improves the area under the learning curve over uniform sampling and CGPO at no extra generation cost, and lies above both baselines in nAULC under four held-out reward models and on DPG-Bench and T2I-CompBench++, which it is not trained on.
blocks.zh: 我们把文本对图像模型的偏好调整设定为三个独立的组件 — — 效用、估计器和批量选择 — — 并提出SPROUT, 其基于目标的效用是偏好目标从一个急用组产生的梯度规范。 通过在线只使用文本的模型校正,从即时文本中预言了这种效用,并且以从预想的效用缩放的概率来接受提示。 SPROUT在不到一半的迭代中达到统一的采样GenEval最终分数,比统一采样和CGPO改善学习曲线下的区域,无需额外的生成成本,并在4个被搁置的奖励模式下在NAULC和DPG-Bench和T2I-CompBench++上都高于基线.

blocks.en: Limitations. Our experiments use a single backbone (Stable Diffusion 1.5), preference objective (DGPO) and training reward (the partial-credit GenEval reward). In the low-budget setting we focus on, the update norm gives a larger gain in GenEval nAULC and reduction factor than the reward variance, although the interval of the nAULC difference includes zero. The reward variance may work better with larger budgets (Appendix C ), and with B = 16 B=16 and over 200 iterations the GenEval gains hold on the seed mean while their intervals include zero (Appendices G and I ). Predictors that rank prompts better offline did not always improve training (Appendix H ), and prompt selection beyond 100 iterations requires a decaying learning rate to stay stable (Appendix I ). We leave these directions for future work.

blocks.en: CGPO. We implement CGPO following its released code: a prompt-specific estimate of the reward variance, calibrated per GenEval task category as in the paper, turned into a batch by the same rejection sampling. CGPO’s other techniques belong to its prompt-specific estimator: every prompt not measured in a round has its probability raised by an exploration increment, and each probability is averaged with its two previous values. The category calibration is the only place where task labels enter training and is only used by CGPO.

A Position or Attribute prompt has two requirements, and few images meet both ( 5.5 % 5.5\% to 8.2 % 8.2\% of the training images of these prompts), so the reward of these prompts mostly shows whether the named objects appear. SPROUT favors prompts whose images receive different rewards (Appendix E ), so it trains more on images with and without the named objects. Position remains hard for every method, since it also requires the correct placement; still, SPROUT reaches the highest Position and Attribute scores ( 0.08 0.08 and 0.12 0.12 ). blocks.en: Figure 7 shows which prompts SPROUT favors and which it avoids. At iterations 21, 41, 61 and 81 of each of the three seeds, we take the twelve prompts with the highest and the twelve with the lowest predicted utility, generate 24 24 images for each from the model of the preceding iteration with the training sampler settings, and score them with the training reward; the figure shows one selected prompt per iteration from each set. Prompts drawn uniformly from the pool lie in between, with a within-prompt standard deviation of 0.227 0.227 . The utility model is fit on update norms, not on rewards or their variance, yet the prompts it ranks highest are those whose images the reward separates, which is the within-group contrast that the preference objective learns from (Section 3.2 ): images whose rewards differ receive nonzero advantages, whereas a group with equal rewards contributes only through the penalty to the reference model.

blocks.en: Table 13 asks whether a stronger predictor helps, with every other setting as in Table 11 . Against the ridge regression with α = 10 \alpha=10 used throughout the paper, we test ridge with α = 1000 \alpha=1000 for the variance utility and, for the update norm, the CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder with a new 768 768 – 256 256 – 1 1 head, fine-tuned at every iteration with one pass over all labels so far (learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} for the encoder and 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} for the head). Offline, fitting on earlier iterations of B = 8 B=8 runs and predicting the prompts trained at the next, both rank prompts better than ridge with α = 10 \alpha=10 (Spearman 0.224 0.224 against 0.171 0.171 for the variance utility and 0.215 0.215 against 0.077 0.077 for the update norm). This ranking is almost entirely of prompts without a label of their own: 98.5 % 98.5\% of the prompts that SPROUT trains on with B = 8 B=8 had never been trained on earlier in the same run, and on these prompts the Spearman correlation between the utility model’s prediction at selection time and the label is 0.027 0.027 in iterations 2–20 and 0.166 0.166 in iterations 81–100. blocks.en: To see whether the gains persist, we resume each B = 8 B=8 run from its state at iteration 100 and continue to iteration 200. At a constant learning rate, prompt selection becomes unstable: three of the six runs of SPROUT and SPROUT w/ variance collapse, falling more than 0.02 0.02 below their own best at two consecutive checkpoints, against neither of the two uniform-sampling runs extended. Every method in Table 14 and Figure 9 therefore decays the learning rate after iteration 100, by a cosine to 0.3 × 0.3\times at iteration 120 and a second cosine to zero at iteration 200. Under this schedule none of our runs collapses, while CGPO collapses on one seed, and SPROUT w/ variance and SPROUT keep their lead over uniform sampling, at 0.504 0.504 and 0.507 0.507 against 0.497 0.497 at iteration 200. Their nAULC gains of 12.8 × 10 − 3 12.8\times 10^{-3} have intervals that include zero, with SPROUT ahead on all three seeds and SPROUT w/ variance on two.
